# Spit, don't rinse {#sec-spit}

Of the three brushing recommendations I audited as blog posts, this is the one
where the guideline comes off best and where I come off worst. DBOH rates the
evidence for it **moderate**, which is higher than for frequency or timing, and
when I went back to the primary trial to check that rating, I found it was not
the trial I had described.

## The advice

> - spitting out after brushing rather than rinsing with water, to avoid diluting
>   the fluoride concentration
>
> Strength of recommendation: **Strong**
>
> --- *Delivering Better Oral Health*, chapter 2, tables 1b, 1d and 1f
> [@dboh2025]

## What the guideline says its evidence is

For children aged 3 to 6:

> Recommendation based on moderate certainty for toothbrushing with fluoride
> toothpaste, for fluoride concentration for permanent teeth (evidence around
> primary teeth less clear) and **spitting versus rinsing**.
>
> --- *Delivering Better Oral Health*, chapter 13, table 2 [@dboh2025]

For adults:

> **Moderate certainty from studies with children and adolescents** for spitting
> versus rinsing.
>
> --- *Delivering Better Oral Health*, chapter 13, table 6 [@dboh2025]

Moderate is a serious rating. In GRADE it means we are reasonably confident the
true effect is close to the estimate, and that further research is more likely to
refine it than reverse it. It is the same rating DBOH gives fluoride toothpaste
itself.

The citation is SIGN 138, whose §5.7.1 grades this **A** and rests on two
studies: a Swedish randomised trial [@sjogren1995] and a Scottish analysis
[@chestnutt1998].

## The Swedish trial, read properly

Here is what I wrote about it in 2023:

> In the Swedish one, 131 4-year-old children were instructed to rinse the
> remaining toothpaste in their mouth with a sip of water for a minute. Compared
> to no instruction, on average, 0.41 less decayed or filled tooth surface was
> seen after 3 years.

And elsewhere in the same series I gave the number as 369. Both numbers are in
the literature, and I had not worked out why. The answer matters, so here it is.

There are two Sjögren publications from 1995. One is a doctoral thesis published
as a supplement to the *Swedish Dental Journal*, which reports several
sub-studies together [@sjogren1995thesis]. The other is the peer-reviewed report
of the trial itself, in *Caries Research* [@sjogren1995], and it is the one SIGN
cites. In that trial:

- **369** four-year-olds were randomised, to **four** groups;
- **281 (76%)** completed at age seven;
- of the completers, **131** were in the two test groups and **150** in the two
  control groups.

So 369 is the randomised total and 131 is the number of *completers* in the test
arms. Neither figure is wrong; I had used each without the other.

The 24% attrition is worth pausing on. Reporting group sizes as the number who
finished, rather than the number randomised, means the published analysis is not
by intention to treat, and 88 children left the study without our knowing which
way they went.

But the far more important thing is what the intervention actually was.

::: {.callout-important title="What the test group was told to do"}
Verbatim from the trial report [@sjogren1995], the test groups were instructed:

1. to spread the paste evenly on the teeth prior to brushing;
2. **not to expectorate more than necessary during brushing**;
3. **to filter the remaining dentifrice foam in the dentition, together with a
   sip of water, by active cheek movements for 1 minute before expectorating**;
4. **not to carry out any further water rinsings afterwards, and not to eat or
   drink for 2 hours after brushing.**
:::

Read item 3 again. The children in the test group were told to take a sip of
water and swill the toothpaste foam around their mouth for a full minute.

They were told to **rinse**. With toothpaste slurry, deliberately, as a
mouthwash.

So the trial DBOH cites as moderate-certainty evidence for "spit, don't rinse"
is a trial of a four-part technique in which one part is a form of rinsing, one
part is not eating or drinking for two hours afterwards, and one part is how you
apply the paste in the first place. Only item 4's second clause corresponds to
what a modern reader understands by "don't rinse."

This is [Chapter -@sec-bundling]'s problem again, one level further down. The
guideline bundles six instructions and lets the best-evidenced one carry the
label. The trial underneath bundles four behaviours and reports one result. You
cannot get from that result to any single component.

And the "no eating or drinking for two hours" instruction is not incidental. If
that alone drove the effect, the correct advice would be different from the
advice being given, and nobody could tell from this trial.

The result itself is real: the test groups developed a mean of 1.14 new
approximal decayed and filled surfaces over three years against 1.55 in the
controls, p<0.05, a relative reduction of about 26%. The 0.41 in my blog post is
the difference between those two numbers. The trial report gives no confidence
interval for it, which is of its time and is why I cannot give one here either.

::: {.callout-note title="How I judged this: risk of bias" collapse="true"}
Assessed with RoB 2, for the effect of assignment to the intervention.

*Randomisation process.* The report states children were randomly assigned to
four groups but gives no detail of sequence generation or allocation concealment.
Baseline balance is reported. **Some concerns**, not high: the absence of
reported detail in a 1995 paper is weaker evidence of a problem than it would be
today.

*Deviations from intended interventions.* The trial is described as double-blind,
which refers to the two toothpastes. It cannot be blind for the technique
instruction, since the instruction is the intervention. Adherence to a four-part
daily behaviour over three years in four-year-olds is unlikely to have been
complete and is not reported. **High.**

*Missing outcome data.* 24% did not complete, results are reported on completers,
and there is no analysis of whether attrition differed by group. **High.**

*Measurement of the outcome.* Approximal lesions scored on bitewing radiographs,
restricted to the distal surface of the first and mesial surface of the second
primary molars. Radiographic scoring is reasonably objective, but examiner
blinding to group is not reported. **Some concerns.**

*Selection of the reported result.* No protocol available. **Some concerns.**

**Overall: high risk of bias.** This agrees with the conclusion I reached in
2023, though for partly different reasons, and it sits awkwardly with DBOH's
rating of moderate certainty. Full domain judgments in the appraisal data.
:::

## The Scottish study

SIGN's second source is Chestnutt and colleagues, 1998 [@chestnutt1998]. As I
noted in the blog post, and as its own title says, this is an analysis of "the
influence of toothbrushing frequency and post-brushing rinsing on caries
experience **in a caries clinical trial**."

The trial it sits inside was designed to compare toothpastes with and without
zinc citrate. Rinsing behaviour was not randomised. It was self-reported at
interview, with participants shown a board of sketches and asked which of four
methods they used: transferring water with the toothbrush, putting the mouth
under the tap, using cupped hands, or using a beaker.

The reported result is that adolescents who said they used a beaker had a caries
increment of 6.84 against 5.84 in those who did not, p<0.05: one more decayed,
missing or filled surface.

Three problems, in increasing order of seriousness.

**It is observational.** Whatever the trial's randomisation achieved, it did not
achieve balance on rinsing habit. Comparing beaker users with non-users is
comparing groups that chose their own exposure, in a population where oral
hygiene habits track socioeconomic position closely.

**The four categories became two.** The authors collapsed the four rinsing
methods into beaker versus everything else, on the stated grounds that three of
them gave similar results. Deciding on a grouping after seeing the results is
selective analysis, or analysis specified after the fact.

In the blog post I called this "p-hacking." I have changed that. P-hacking
usually means trying analyses until one crosses a significance threshold, and I
have no evidence that is what happened here. Collapsing categories because they
look alike is a defensible exploratory move; the failure is presenting the result
as if it had been planned, and citing it as though it were a trial result.

**Confounding.** The four groups differ at baseline in caries experience and in
sex distribution. If you were designing this analysis today you would specify a
causal model and adjust for the common causes of both rinsing habit and caries.

::: {.callout-note title="What you would need to adjust for" collapse="true"}
Drawing the directed acyclic graph for "does using a beaker cause caries" gives a
minimal adjustment set of socioeconomic position, age, sex and parental
education: each plausibly influences both the choice of rinsing method and the
caries outcome, and none lies on the causal path between them.

Two cautions I did not give in the blog version. Adjusting for a variable that
sits *between* rinsing and caries, such as fluoride concentration retained in the
mouth, would block the very effect we want to estimate. And adjusting for a
variable caused by both, such as overall oral hygiene score, could open a path
rather than close one. "Control for everything you measured" is not a method.

None of this is available without the individual data, so this remains a
statement about what the study cannot tell us rather than a re-analysis.
:::

## Where does "moderate" come from?

This is the honest difficulty of the chapter.

I can see how one gets to low certainty: one randomised trial at high risk of
bias, testing a bundle, plus one observational analysis with post-hoc grouping.
I cannot reconstruct a route to **moderate** from these two studies, and DBOH
does not show its working beyond the one-line statement.

There are two possibilities and I cannot distinguish between them from the
published document. Either the panel considered evidence not listed in chapter
13's reference for this row, or moderate is the rating for the bundle as a whole,
carried by fluoride toothpaste, and the phrase "and spitting versus rinsing"
extends it further than the underlying evidence reaches.

I lean towards the second, because the same sentence rates three different things
at once. But I want to be clear that this is an inference about a document, not a
finding about the evidence, and I would withdraw it if the panel published its
reasoning.

::: {.callout-note title="What I searched, and when" collapse="true"}
PubMed, 15 August 2026, for randomised trials of post-brushing water rinsing.
Four records, all screened in full. Full strategy and screening decisions in
`appraisals/searches/ch07-post-brushing-rinsing.md`.

**No randomised trial isolating post-brushing rinsing with a caries outcome was
found.** Everything published since 2000 measures salivary fluoride retention,
which is the same surrogate problem as [Chapter -@sec-last-thing]:

- A crossover in 10 adults found higher salivary fluoride for up to 30 minutes
  without rinsing, and no significant difference in systemic absorption, which is
  reassuring on safety [@parakaw2024].
- A randomised trial in 120 adults across 12 arms found rinsing significantly
  affected salivary fluoride retention to 90 minutes [@albahrani2022].
- A crossover in 32 children found the same [@nazzal2016].

These agree with each other and point the right way. They also illustrate the
step this book keeps finding. Nazzal and colleagues conclude that their results
"support the current recommendation" of spitting without rinsing. Their results
are about fluoride in saliva; the recommendation is about tooth decay. That
sentence is where a surrogate quietly becomes a clinical claim.

The nearest thing to a caries outcome is an in-situ study using orthodontic
bands and quantitative light-induced fluorescence [@almulla2010]. Its test
regimen was 5,000ppm fluoride **and** no rinsing, against a control of 1,450ppm
**with** three rinses. Two things were changed at once, so the result cannot be
attributed to the rinsing. It is the confounded-comparison problem of the
Swedish trial, repeated fifteen years later.
:::

::: {.verdict}
[Verdict]{.verdict-title}

Certainty of evidence
:   [Low]{.certainty .low}. One randomised trial at high risk of bias which
    tested a four-part bundle rather than rinsing alone, plus one non-randomised
    within-trial analysis with post-hoc regrouping. This is one rating below
    DBOH's stated moderate, and I cannot reconstruct how moderate was reached.

    In the blog version I said "very low." I have moved up, not down: there is a
    randomised trial here with a caries outcome pointing in the right direction,
    which is more than either of the two preceding chapters can say.

Directness to the advice as worded
:   **Moderate.** The Swedish trial has the right population, a
    patient-relevant outcome and a three-year follow-up. Its intervention is a
    bundle of which not rinsing is one part, so the effect cannot be attributed
    to the advice as worded. The Scottish analysis is indirect on design.

Is the strength label defensible?
:   **Arguably yes, unlike the previous two chapters.** This is the best
    candidate in the brushing bundle for a legitimate discordant recommendation:
    the intervention is free, has no plausible harm, the mechanism is clear, and
    the one randomised trial points the right way. A Strong recommendation on
    low-certainty evidence is defensible here. What is not defensible is stating
    the certainty as moderate without showing how.

What would change my mind
:   A trial randomising people to rinse or not rinse after brushing, with
    everything else identical, and caries measured at two years or more. That is
    a cheap, ethical, entirely feasible trial that nobody has run in thirty
    years. Alternatively, publication of the reasoning behind DBOH's moderate
    rating would settle whether I have simply missed something the panel saw.
:::

## What this means for you

Spit, don't rinse. Of the three pieces of brushing advice in this part of the
book, this is the one I would defend most readily: it is the only one with a
randomised trial behind it, that trial found less decay, and there is no
conceivable downside to not reaching for a glass of water.

Two honest caveats. The trial that supports it also told children not to eat or
drink for two hours afterwards, and nobody knows how much of the benefit came
from that instead. And the children in that trial did swill toothpaste foam
around their mouths for a minute, so if you want to follow what was actually
tested, "spit, don't rinse" is not quite it.
